description: How myth explained the founding of cities — Athena and Poseidon's contest for Athens, and Romulus and Remus at Rome.
content_html:
Why Cities Needed Foundation Myths

Every great city of the ancient world told stories about how it came to exist. These were not simply fairy tales: foundation myths gave a city its identity, its prestige and its claim to divine protection. They answered the question “why are we here, and why does this city deserve to flourish?” by anchoring the answer in the actions of gods and heroes. Athens claimed the goddess Athena as its patron; Rome traced its ancestry to the Trojan hero Aeneas and through him to the goddess Venus. These stories were told and retold in art, literature and public ritual — they shaped how citizens understood their city and its place in the world.

The Naming of Athens: Athena and Poseidon

The Athenians told a story of a divine contest for their city. Two Olympians — Athena and Poseidon — both wanted to be patron of the new city, and Zeus ruled that the one who gave the most useful gift to the citizens would win. Poseidon struck the ground of the Acropolis with his trident and a spring of salt water gushed forth — powerful, dramatic, a reminder of his dominion over the sea. Athena struck the earth and an olive tree grew. The citizens (in some versions, judged by the gods; in others, by the people themselves, with the women voting for Athena) chose the olive tree, and Athena became the city’s patron. The city was named Athens in her honour.

The olive tree was enormously meaningful to Greek life: olive oil was food, fuel for lamps, and a sacred substance used in religious ritual and to anoint the bodies of athletes. Athena’s gift was practical where Poseidon’s was merely impressive. The myth encoded a civic value: wisdom and usefulness matter more than raw power. The sacred olive tree on the Acropolis was tended as a holy relic for centuries. Ancient sources reported that when the Persians burned Athens in 480 BC, the tree sprouted new shoots the very next day — a sign, the Athenians said, of Athena’s undying protection.

Key Fact

The contest between Athena and Poseidon was depicted on the west pediment of the Parthenon, the most prominent sculptural programme in Athens. Both deities were shown at the moment of the contest, flanked by the Olympian gods as witnesses. By placing this myth at the heart of their most sacred building, the Athenians permanently embedded their divine foundation story in stone.

Theseus and the Adventures of Athens’s Hero-King

Athens also celebrated Theseus, its own heroic founder-king, whose adventures were displayed on the Theseus Kylix, now in the British Museum (catalogue number 1850,0302.3). This red-figure cup, made around 440 BC, shows seven episodes in total: the Minotaur at the centre (tondo), and six bandit and monster encounters on the outer ring — Kerkyon, Prokrustes, Skiron, the Bull of Marathon, Sinis and the Krommyonian Sow. The cup is a striking example of how a single portable object could carry an entire heroic biography. The choice of adventures depicted sends a political message: Theseus makes the roads and the sea safe, he defeats the monstrous enemy, he brings civilisation — just as Athens itself claimed to do for the Greek world.

The Founding of Rome: Romulus and Remus

Rome’s foundation myth was recorded by the historian Livy in his Early History of Rome (Book 1). According to Livy, the twins Romulus and Remus were descended from the Trojan hero Aeneas through the line of kings of Alba Longa. Their mother was a Vestal Virgin, Rhea Silvia, who had been made a priestess to prevent her from having children (and thus potential heirs who might threaten the king). The god Mars, however, came to her and fathered the twins — giving Rome its legendary divine ancestry through the god of war.

The king ordered the infants to be drowned in the Tiber, but the river was in flood and the basket carrying them was set down on dry land instead, at the foot of the Palatine Hill. There, according to Livy, a she-wolf found the abandoned infants and suckled them; later they were found and raised by a shepherd and his wife. When they grew up, they overthrew the wicked king and decided to found their own city. A dispute arose over which of two hills to build it on, and an argument about the omens (Romulus saw twelve vultures; Remus saw six) led to Romulus killing Remus. Romulus then built Rome and became its first king.

Key Fact

Livy presents the Romulus and Remus myth as reflecting key Roman values: the twins were suckled by a she-wolf (strength and ferocity), raised by a shepherd (humble origins, closeness to the land), and their divine father was Mars (Rome’s military destiny). The killing of Remus was a disturbing detail, but it established that Rome would have one founder, one king, one destiny — not a divided city.

Aeneas and the Trojan Origins of Rome

Before Romulus and Remus, Rome traced its ultimate origins even further back, to Aeneas, a Trojan prince and son of the goddess Venus. Livy records that after the fall of Troy, Aeneas led a band of survivors westward, eventually arriving in Italy and founding a settlement at Alba Longa, whose line of kings eventually included Rhea Silvia — and thus Romulus and Remus. This Trojan origin story served a brilliant political function: it made Rome part of the Greek mythological world (Troy was a major player in the greatest of all Greek myths, the Trojan War) while simultaneously asserting Roman independence — they were not Greek, they were Trojans, the Greeks’ defeated enemies, reborn as something far greater. Virgil’s Aeneid made this origin story the national epic of Rome.

Plutarch, writing in the late first century AD, wrote biographies of famous Greeks and Romans in parallel pairs, each pair exploring a Greek and a Roman who shared similar qualities or roles. He paired Theseus (founder of Athens as a unified city) with Romulus (founder of Rome) and wrote an explicit comparison of the two. Plutarch noted that both heroes had uncertain births (divine or semi-divine fathers, mothers of uncertain status), both unified scattered communities into a single great city, and both committed acts of violence — Theseus abandoning Ariadne; Romulus killing Remus — that cast a shadow over their achievements. Plutarch’s comparison is a sophisticated literary work that invites readers to think about what kind of character a founder needs and what moral compromises city-building demands. For this exam, the key use of Plutarch is to show that ancient authors themselves compared Athens and Rome through their foundation heroes.

Modern historians do not take the stories of Romulus and Remus or the contest of Athena and Poseidon as literal history. However, there is real archaeological evidence for early settlement at Rome and Athens. The question is not “did it happen?” but “what did the myth mean?” Foundation myths told citizens who they were, who their city belonged to, and what values it stood for. They were performed in drama, displayed in public art, and recited in religious ceremonies. Even Livy, writing a careful history of Rome, included the Romulus and Remus story while acknowledging that such tales “adorn” the origins of cities — he did not expect his readers to believe every detail literally, but he recognised that the stories shaped Roman identity in ways no dry list of facts could replace.
exam_tip_html: Foundation myth questions often ask you to ‘explain’ what a myth meant to a city or to ‘analyse’ a source. The key analytical move is to ask: what values does this myth celebrate? The Athena–Poseidon contest celebrates wisdom and usefulness over brute force; the Romulus and Remus story celebrates martial strength, divine parentage (Mars), and unified singular leadership. For source analysis questions on the Theseus Kylix or a passage from Livy, use specific details from the source and explain their significance, then link them to the broader function of the myth. A common essay question asks you to compare the Athenian and Roman foundation stories — always use named sources (the Parthenon west pediment; the Theseus Kylix; Livy; Plutarch’s Parallel Lives) to back your points.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Foundation myths gave cities divine prestige and civic identity: Athens was named after Athena (who won a contest against Poseidon), while Rome traced its origins to Romulus (son of Mars and descendant of the Trojan hero Aeneas).
  • Key sources include the west pediment of the Parthenon (Athena–Poseidon contest), the Theseus Kylix in the British Museum, Livy’s account of Romulus and Remus, and Plutarch’s comparison of Theseus and Romulus in his Parallel Lives.
  • Both myths encode the values of their city: Athens celebrated wisdom and practical gifts; Rome celebrated divine military lineage (Mars as father), humble origins and the singular strength of one founder’s vision.

practice_questions.text: Name the goddess who won the contest to become patron of Athens.
Describe the scenes shown on the Theseus Kylix.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three accurate details: it is a red-figure drinking cup (kylix); it is now in the British Museum; it dates to around 440 BC; it shows seven episodes — the Minotaur at the centre (tondo) and six bandit/monster encounters on the outer ring; scenes include Theseus defeating Kerkyon, Prokrustes, Skiron, the Bull of Marathon, Sinis and the Krommyonian Sow; Theseus killing the Minotaur is the central tondo scene; it is a portable object that carries a heroic biography.

practice_questions.text:
Read the following passage, which paraphrases a section of an ancient historian's account of Rome's foundation:

The twins were placed in a basket and set afloat on the flooded Tiber, but the water receded and left them on dry ground at the foot of a hill. A she-wolf found them there and suckled them with her milk. In this way the founders of the greatest city in the world were kept alive by a wild beast of the forest.

Using the passage and your own knowledge, explain what this story reveals about how the Romans wanted their city to be understood.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5): Analyses at least three specific elements with precise own-knowledge support. The she-wolf: strength, ferocity, connection to the wild (Rome born of nature’s power, not weakness); divine intervention implied (Mars as their father; the gods ensured they survived); the Palatine Hill setting (the heart of later Rome; the story ties origins to the city’s physical geography); the impossible survival against orders = destiny, divine protection. Identifies this as Livy’s account and evaluates what the mythologising of origins reveals about Roman national identity (military destiny, divine legitimacy, resilience). Reaches a conclusion about what the myth ‘does’ for Rome.
Secure (4): Analyses two elements with clear explanation; names Livy; some argument about Roman values.
Developing (3): Identifies one or two details; descriptive rather than fully analytical.
Emerging (1–2): Retells the story; little or no analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Trojan origin myth of Aeneas was important to Roman identity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the basic claim (Aeneas, a Trojan hero and son of Venus, was ancestor of the Roman people); 1 mark for explaining the political usefulness (it gave Rome a place in the Greek mythological world while asserting independence from Greece; it connected Rome to the goddess Venus); 1 mark for the literary significance (Virgil’s Aeneid made it the national epic); 1 mark for connecting to Augustus (Augustus claimed descent through Julius Caesar to Aeneas and thus Venus, using the myth for imperial propaganda).

practice_questions.text: 'The foundation myths of Athens and Rome served the same purpose but reflected very different values.' How far do you agree? Use a range of named sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9–10): Sustained argument engaging with both agreement and disagreement. Same purpose: both myths gave divine legitimacy, civic identity and national prestige; both linked the city to the gods; both were displayed publicly (Parthenon pediment; Ara Pacis Aeneas panel). Different values: Athens prized wisdom and practical skills (olive over salt spring; Athena over Poseidon); Rome prized military strength and destiny (Mars as father; she-wolf; killing Remus = singular decisive leadership). Comparison enriched by Plutarch’s Parallel Lives (Theseus and Romulus as founding heroes with different but parallel characteristics). Uses multiple named sources (Parthenon west pediment; Theseus Kylix; Livy Book 1; Plutarch; Virgil Aeneid; Ara Pacis). Reaches a well-supported judgement.
Secure (7–8): Clear argument on both sides with some named sources and a reasonable conclusion.
Developing (5–6): Some relevant points; limited source use; conclusion may be undeveloped.
Emerging (1–4): One-sided or descriptive; sources absent.

practice_questions.text: Give two details from the Romulus and Remus myth that gave Rome a sense of divine destiny.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: their father was Mars, the god of war; they were suckled by a she-wolf (wild strength, divine protection); they survived against the orders of the king (gods kept them alive); Romulus saw the superior omen of twelve vultures (divine sanction for his city); their ancestry ran back to Aeneas and the goddess Venus.

The contest between Athena and Poseidon for Athens was depicted on the _____ pediment of the Parthenon.

First king and founder of Rome
Hero-king of Athens depicted on the Theseus Kylix

flashcard_questions.q: What did Poseidon offer in the contest for the city of Athens?
flashcard_questions.a: A spring of salt water, struck from the Acropolis with his trident.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did the Athenians choose Athena's gift over Poseidon's?
flashcard_questions.a: An olive tree was more useful — providing food, oil and sacred substance — than a salt spring.

flashcard_questions.q: What visual source in the British Museum depicts the adventures of Theseus?
flashcard_questions.a: The Theseus Kylix (a red-figure drinking cup, c.440 BC).

flashcard_questions.q: Who was the divine father of Romulus and Remus, according to Roman tradition?
How did Romulus and Remus survive being abandoned as infants?
flashcard_questions.a: A she-wolf found and suckled them.

flashcard_questions.q: Who recorded the story of Romulus and Remus in his Early History of Rome?

flashcard_questions.a: A story explaining the divine origin of a city, linking it to gods and heroic ancestors.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was the Trojan origin of Rome (Aeneas) important to the Romans?
flashcard_questions.a: It connected Rome to Greek myth and the goddess Venus while asserting an independent identity from Greece.

flashcard_questions.q: On which building was the contest of Athena and Poseidon depicted in sculpted form?
flashcard_questions.a: The west pediment of the Parthenon.

flashcard_questions.q: In Plutarch's Parallel Lives, which founding heroes are compared — one Greek and one Roman?

glossary_terms.definition: Stories explaining the origin and divine sanction of a city or people, linking the community to the gods and to heroic ancestors.
A tree on the Acropolis of Athens believed to be the very tree that Athena caused to grow in her contest with Poseidon; tended as a holy object for centuries.
The national hero of Athens; son of King Aegeus, famous for killing the Minotaur and defeating six bandits and monsters; depicted on the Theseus Kylix in the British Museum.

A red-figure drinking cup (kylix) now in the British Museum showing seven episodes from the adventures of Theseus: the Minotaur at the centre and six bandit/monster encounters on the outer ring; a key prescribed visual source.
The Trojan hero who fled the fall of Troy, led his people to Italy, and became the ancestor of the Roman people; his story is told in Virgil's Aeneid.
